full_judgment:
5. The defendant No. 1 petitioner is now aggrieved by the impugned appellate Judgment and decree primarily by reason that the said judgment and decree of reversal do not benefit from well-reasoned findings and decision as mandated under Order XLI, rules 31 and 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure (hereinafter referred to as the 'Code'). In this regard, the defendant No. 1-petitioner submits that the lower appellate Court lost sight of the fact that the Kabala in question is registered as proven by evidence adduced in the form of statements given by competent and reliable witnesses, and instead concerned itself with issues of payment and alleged improper execution by ignoring other material evidence regarding the same as otherwise duly and properly considered by the trial Court. The sum total of the petitioner's grievance lies in the fact that the impugned judgment and decree are replete with surmises and conjectures not based on evidence and material on record thereby leading to a misreading of evidence resulting in an error of law and decision occasioning failure of justice. On behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party, it is generally submitted that the evidence adduced by her before both the courts below reflect a wide web of deceit spun by the defendant No. 1 petitioner taking advantage of the vulnerability of the plaintiff-opposite party by reason of her physical infirmity i.e., her blindness, and the fact she is a divorcee who who had no male relation living with her at the time. 

 "It appears that the High Court Division has come to the conclusion that the judgment of the appellate Court suffers from illegality resulting in the error in the decision occasioning a failure of justice. In coming to this conclusion the said Court has noticed that the judgment of the appellate Court was not a proper judgment of reversal, inasmuch as the learned Subordinate Judge did not consider the material facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence taken into consideration by the trial Court nor did he advert to its reasoning or reverse the material findings of the said Court. The High Court Division has further noticed that there was practically no evidence, either documentary or circumstantial, in support of the defendants' claim of surrender of the tenancy by the CS recorded tenants in favour of the landlords and the settlement of the suit land with them. But the appellate Court missed these material aspects of the case. In our opinion, the High Court Division has given cogent reasons for reversing the judgment of the appellate Court."
